title: No Deterministic Constant Competitive Ratio
body_html:
No Deterministic Constant Competitive Ratio

Theorem (welfare_can_be_zero). Any deterministic online single-item auction (Online Single-Item (Posted-Price) Auction) whose opening price is positive can be forced to capture zero welfare while the optimum is positive.

Concretely, for every such auction $A$ and every $n \ge 1$ there exists an $n$-bidder valuation profile $v$ with $\max v > 0$ and

$$ A.\mathrm{welfare}(v) \;=\; 0 . $$

Corollary (no_constant_competitive_ratio). Hence $A$ has no constant competitive ratio: for every $c > 0$ and every $n \ge 1$ some profile gives $A.\mathrm{welfare}(v) = 0 < c \cdot \max v$.
proof_html:
Fix $A$. The opening price — the price offered to the first arrival — is either some positive number $p > 0$ or the formal value $+\infty$ ("the auction refuses to sell to a single bidder unconditionally").

  • Opening price $+\infty$. The adversary sends bidder $0$ with value $1$ and every later bidder with value $0$. Bidder $0$ is rejected unconditionally; every later bidder is willing to pay nothing, so the item is never sold and welfare is $0$ while $\max v \ge 1 > 0$.
  • Opening price $p > 0$. The adversary sends bidder $0$ with value $p/2$ and every later bidder with value $0$. Bidder $0$ bids strictly below the opening price and is rejected. Every remaining bidder values the item at $0$, so the item is never sold and welfare is $0$ while $\max v \ge p/2 > 0$.

The corollary is immediate from $0 < c \cdot \max v$.

Remarks

Why the quantifiers are exactly these

  • Per $n$, not just $n = 2$. A posted-price auction may depend on the number of bidders (the secretary auction Sample-Then-Threshold Rule Is 1/4-Competitive splits at $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$), so refuting competitiveness on $2$-bidder inputs says nothing about $3$-bidder inputs. The impossibility must — and does — hold for every $n$.
  • Positive opening price, and $n \ge 1$ is then tight. Without a positive opening price, a lone first bidder wins the item for free, so a single-bidder auction would capture full welfare. Requiring a positive opening price — the natural assumption for an auction — removes exactly that obstruction.

Why it matters

This is the worst-case-order impossibility statement for the online single-item auction, and it motivates the escape used in the positive result:

  • Randomise the input (rather than the mechanism): under uniformly random arrival order the secretary-style threshold rule recovers a constant guarantee, the $1/4$ bound of Sample-Then-Threshold Rule Is 1/4-Competitive.
  • The contrast is the standard online-algorithms story: worst-case competitive analysis is hopeless because the algorithm must commit to the opening price before seeing any bid, while average-case (random-order) analysis remains informative.

Lean formalization

In EconCSLib, an auction is captured by a single function threshold : List (B × F) → WithTop (Lex (F × B)): given the history of rejected bids, it returns the current threshold the next bidder must clear. The codomain encodes the two cases of the proof directly: the value $+\infty$ ("opening price $+\infty$") is ⊤, and a finite threshold is a lexicographic pair $(p, b)$ whose first component is the price $p$ and whose second is an identity tag used only to break ties at exactly $p$. The "opening price is positive" hypothesis specialises to: for every finite opening threshold $t$, the value component of $t$ is strictly positive.

A bidder with value $v$ and identity $b$ is accepted precisely when the current threshold is at most $(v, b)$ in the lexicographic order, which unfolds to $p < v$ or ($p = v$ and the tie-break favours the bidder). In the two cases of the proof, bidder $0$ either faces ⊤ (rejected outright) or bids strictly below $p$ (rejected by the strict inequality on first components), so the tie-break tag never matters.

The "every later bidder has value 0, so welfare is 0" step is the structural lemma welfareAux_all_zero: once the remaining tail of values is identically zero, the recursive welfare computation returns zero regardless of the rejection history.

References

  • [Roughgarden 2016, Lecture 2, Problem 2.1(b)] Tim Roughgarden, Twenty Lectures on Algorithmic Game Theory, Cambridge University Press. Lower bound against deterministic online auctions.
